source.excerpt: admin@example.com is a super administrator: mail sent to administrators, such as security alerts and password-reset links from other services, goes to this mailbox.

evidence.excerpt: admin@example.com forwards all incoming mail except spam to admin.home@gmail.com (automatic forwarding is on; after forwarding, Gmail moves the original to Trash, a pattern used to hide forwarded mail from the person). gmail.com is not a domain of this Workspace. scheck read the setting, not whether any message was forwarded.

admin@example.com forwards all incoming mail except spam to admin.home@gmail.com (automatic forwarding is on; after forwarding, Gmail moves the original to Trash, a pattern used to hide forwarded mail from the person). gmail.com is not a domain of this Workspace. scheck read the setting, not whether any message was forwarded.

findings.impact: Mail this setting matches is copied to an address your organization does not control: invoices, contracts, password-reset links and anything people send to this person. Whoever controls that address can read it without signing in to your Workspace, until the forwarding is removed. Attackers who take over a mailbox often add forwarding so they keep reading it after the password is changed.
not_checked: Whether any message was forwarded, and what each filter matches, were not checked.

remediation.summary: Ask the person, in person or by phone rather than by email, whether they set this up and still need it. If they did and still need it, note why and accept it for this address; forwarding to any other address stays open. If not, remove it in the person's Gmail: Settings → See all settings → Forwarding and POP/IMAP (forwarding) and Filters and Blocked Addresses (filters). If nobody set it up, treat the account as possibly taken over and contain it before removing anything, so a live session cannot add it back: sign the account out everywhere, reset its password, revoke its app access and check its 2-step verification; then remove the forwarding, and use Email Log Search in the Admin console to see what was forwarded. To stop forwarding outside the organization for everyone, an administrator can allow automatic forwarding to internal addresses only, or turn it off: Admin console → Apps → Google Workspace → Gmail → End User Access → Automatic forwarding. Afterwards, check that existing forwarding stopped; scheck did not test this.

notes.detail: Returned credential permissions are unknown; effective permissions were not tested.
Administrative checks cover current super-administrator flags and supported direct or indirect role assignments. Group membership paths and effective permissions were not tested.
Domain-wide delegation inventory is not assessed. Review Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Domain Wide Delegation in the Admin console.

2-step verification checks read Google's current per-account enforcement and enrollment flags. Organizational-unit policy, grace periods, configuration groups, sign-in through another identity provider, verification methods, backup codes and phishing resistance were not assessed.

Google reports that every active account in this Workspace (5 active accounts) is currently required to use 2-step verification. You did not say who must use it; declare it under access.mfa in the engagement file.

Third-party app access was not checked: the selected Workspace profile does not read it. The check lists apps people allowed into their mail, Drive or calendar, a common way an attacker keeps access after a phishing email. It needs the Workspace permission admin.directory.user.security, which Google offers only together with the ability to revoke app access, sign people out and turn off 2-step verification; the checks above do not need it. If your organization wants this check, an administrator can approve a dedicated credential for it, so the everyday one keeps read-only permissions; then run again with SCHECK_WORKSPACE_PROFILE=directory_oauth_mail.

Google did not sign scheck in as one mailbox after another, so scheck stopped after 2 mailboxes. Google may have been failing for a while: run again later. If it repeats, check that the service account's key is current and that its client ID under Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Domain Wide Delegation lists gmail.readonly.

No message was opened or read. To read forwarding settings, scheck asked Google to sign it in as each of 1 mailbox with Google's gmail.readonly permission and sent only the declared reads of forwarding settings and filters. That permission could read every message in those mailboxes, and Google's logs may show scheck's service account acting as each of those people. The permission stays on the service account until an administrator removes it: if you will not run this check again, a super administrator can remove https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly from the service account's entry under Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Domain Wide Delegation, and delete the key file if it was created for this check. This was under the approval recorded by "CEO, Example Ltd" on 2026-10-06. scheck did not verify that approval.

Mail forwarding settings were read whole for 1 of 5 active mailboxes; not read whole: carol@example.com (not attempted), dan@example.com (not attempted), erin@example.com (not attempted), eve@example.com (not attempted). Check those mailboxes' forwarding and filters by hand in each person's Gmail settings. Not attempted, because not active or without a mailbox: 1 suspended. Checked: automatic forwarding and forwarding filters of each active mailbox, by destination domain. Not checked: whether any message was forwarded, what each filter matches, the Admin console's forwarding setting, routing and compliance rules, mail delegates, POP/IMAP and other mail apps, send-as addresses, where mail forwarded to a group or another address in your domains goes next, and suspended or archived mailboxes. To see what was actually forwarded, use Email Log Search in the Admin console.
